cur:monumental-santa-prassede-zeno-lamb.summary: In a lunette framed by bands of ornament, the haloed Lamb of God stands on a green mountain from which the rivers of Paradise flow, while two harts approach from either side to drink. The image joins the Lamb of the Apocalypse with the deer of Psalm 42, which 'panteth after the water brooks', a familiar symbol of the soul longing for God.
facts: The Chapel of Saint Zeno was built by Pope Paschal I (817–824) as a funerary chapel for his mother, Theodora; its walls and vault are almost entirely clad in gold-ground mosaic.
Paschal I's mosaics belong to the Carolingian-era revival in Rome, when the pope also translated many martyrs' relics from the catacombs into the city's churches.

cur:objects2-chalice-of-romanos-san-marc.summary: A deep sardonyx cup, mounted in gilded silver and strung with pearls, carries around its rim a band of gold cloisonné enamel plaques with busts of Christ, the Virgin and saints; Christ blesses with his right hand and holds a book. The foot bears the name of an emperor Romanos. Like much of the treasury it probably reached Venice after the sack of Constantinople in 1204; it is one of the masterpieces of Byzantine imperial goldsmith work.
facts: The Romanos named on the chalice is usually identified with Romanos I Lekapenos (920–944) or Romanos II (959–963); the Commons description dates the metalwork 959–963.
The stone cup itself may be much older, possibly a reused late Roman hardstone vessel.
Most of the Byzantine hardstone vessels in the Treasury of San Marco arrived as booty from the Fourth Crusade.
cur:objects2-chalice-of-romanos-san-marc.notes: The emperor's identity (Romanos I or II) is debated; the date here is given broadly as 10th century.

walters:71.244.summary: Christ hangs on the cross with his head bowed and arms outstretched, the sun and moon above and the inscriptions IC XC beside his head. The Virgin, her hands wrapped in her mantle in a gesture of grief, stands at the left; St John, unusually, raises both hands in adoration rather than holding a Gospel book. The faces have been softened by centuries of devout handling.
facts: The Walters notes that the worn faces show the ivory was stroked and rubbed during prayer.
Inscriptions name Christ, the Mother of God and Saint John.
The Crucifixion was one of the most common subjects of Byzantine ivory triptychs; this plaque was the centre of such a devotional object.
